content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors conduct experiments and analyze the feature extractor part of seven models and find that most CIL models overweight stability over plasticity. According to this observation, the authors propose two models based on an existing algorithm. Finally, the authors also find the misalignment between the power of feature extractors and the performance on the standard evaluation metric.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. The techniques and results of analyzing the stability-plasticity dilemma are important and instructive for future CIL work.
2. Experiments in the paper are sufficient and logical. The authors conduct experiments on seven compared methods and two proposed methods with two dataset settings.
3. The authors proposed two simple but efficient algorithms.

Weaknesses
1. The authors proposed two methods, however, it would be better if you can provide a picture to show the framework intuitively.
2. In the sixth part of the paper, you point out the shortcoming of standard evaluation metrics. Your effect would be admired if you can propose an operable evaluation metric based on your observation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Formulas and language expressions of the article are clear and readable. Some necessary charts and tables are also provided.

Quality: The results of most CIL models that overweight stability over plasticity is instructive for future work. But the results of the proposed methods don’t gain significant improvement.

Novelty: The novelty of the work is not enough. The problem-setting and analysis methods of the work are straightforward and well-known. The proposed framework is also mostly based on previous work.
content.summary_of_the_review: Authors design sufficient experiments on the problem of different methods’ stability and plasticity. The observation of the paper is meaningful and instructive for future work. However, the authors just point out some of the observations without giving a way to make full use of them, such as the misalignment between the power of the feature extractor and the performance of the standard evaluation metric. And the proposed methods also don’t gain significant improvement. More work should be done to increase novelty.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a study of the stability-plasticity trade-off in continual learning, focusing mainly on learning and forgetting in the final feature space. The paper first provides two analyses of the feature space learned by existing continual learning methods. First, it studies the expressivity of the feature space by fitting a classifier on the learned feature extractor at different stages in continual learning. Then it analyzes the feature similarity and visualizes the learned features in continual learning. Based on the results, the paper also proposes two simple methods: Partial-DER which applies feature expansion only on the last layer of the network and Exploit that simply takes a fixed feature extractor after the first class and only finetunes the classifier. The results show that the proposed method has comparable or better performance than the existing continual learning method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. The paper provides a good analysis of the evolution of feature space in continual learning. 
2. Based on the study, the authors propose two methods that prove to be simple but have good performance. 
3. The paper is well-written and easy to follow. 

Weaknesses:
1. Although the analysis seems surprising and proposed the method seems very simple but performant, the experiments are very limited and problematic. The only dataset considered in this paper is the full ImageNet with the first incremental learning stage having 500 classes and the following stages each having fewer classes. This means in the proposed setting, the network is “pretrained” on half of the ImageNet and the transfer performance is evaluated. Other popular experimental settings in the CL community typically have a smaller number of images/classes in the initial task, like split CIFAR10 and split CIFAR100. This is not to argue that we should focus on small datasets, but the conclusions reached in the paper may change or reverse on other datasets. Therefore I believe the paper should provide more experiments and results on other datasets. 
2. The paper should compare and contrast its analysis to other existing work on representation forgetting in continual learning [R1, R2], as well as those on pretrained networks [R3, R4]. Some analysis has already existed in the literature. 
3. The proposed methods are too simple, and they only serve as simple baselines in some other papers (e.g. using a fixed pretrained feature extractor in [R3]). They provide little insight into the community. 

[R1] Davari, MohammadReza, et al. "Probing Representation Forgetting in Supervised and Unsupervised Continual Learning." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

[R2] Zhang, Xiao, Dejing Dou, and Ji Wu. "Feature Forgetting in Continual Representation Learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.13359 (2022).

[R3] Mehta, Sanket Vaibhav, et al. "An empirical investigation of the role of pre-training in lifelong learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2112.09153 (2021).

[R4] Cossu, Andrea, et al. "Continual Pre-Training Mitigates Forgetting in Language and Vision." arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.09357 (2022).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This paper is well-written and easy to follow. 

Quality: Overall the quality of the paper is good, but the proposed methods are not interesting and the evaluation is problematic.  

Novelty: The novelty is limited, as detailed in the weakness section.

Reproducibility: The authors did not provide or promise to open source, but the baselines and datasets used in the paper are pretty standard in the CL community. The paper also provides a very detailed description of the implementation.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the analysis seems surprising, I am not convinced since it is evaluated only on a single dataset. The proposed methods are trivial, and the results are not surpassing the baseline by a considerable margin. Also, the paper misses comparison with several similar papers.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is mainly an analysis paper. It experimentally analyzed several existing CIL continual learning systems. It found that existing method favor stability over plasticity and also modified an existing method and achieved better accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
This paper did an experimental analysis of some existing methods, which is useful as not so much work on this has been done so far. 
Inspired by the analysis, two variations of an existing method are proposed and show improved results. 

Weaknesses
(1) Why is it surprising that the feature representations of most CIL models are subject to only trivial variations as the model is trained on incremental data? Isn’t this because existing methods try to protect previous parameters to overcome CF. If you try EWC, you may not observe as much of this because its regularization-based method does not protect much. 

(2) Why is there anything wrong with the protection of previous parameters or favoring stability? A number of methods are based on protection and perform very well, e.g., ITAML [1], CCG [2] and CLOM [3]. It depends on what you protect and whether they should be protected. DER also does protection. 
[1] ITAML: An incremental task-agnostic meta-learning approach. CVPR, 2020
[2] Conditional channel gated networks for task-aware continual learning. CVPR, 2020
[3] Continual Learning Based on OOD Detection and Task Masking. CVPR continual learning workshop, 2022. 

(3) How do you know that your selection of existing methods are representative enough? There are a large number of other systems and approaches. For example, you have not covered the orthogonal projection based methods and those in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. 

(4) Your system has pre-training using 500 classes of ImageNet. Since pretraining has already learned good features, the subsequent tasks may not need to change the feature extractor so much. For your analysis, you should not have used pre-training. Otherwise, the conclusion is questionable. I am not against using pre-trained models as in NLP, about every continual learning system uses a pre-trained transformer. Some computer vision papers are starting to use pre-trained feature extractors too. See the next point.  

(5) But since you are using pre-training, you should have compared with those methods that use a pre-train model (e.g., [4, 5]) rather than systems that are not designed for using a pre-trained model. 
[4]. Learning to prompt for continual learning. CVPR, 2022
[5]. A Multi-Head Model for Continual Learning Via Out-of-Distribution Replay, Collas, 2022. 

(6) The following paper did a theoretical analysis of catastrophic forgetting, which is another angle of looking at the problem. It may give us some guidance in your empirical work. 
[6] A Theoretical Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting through the NTK Overlap Matrix. AISTATS-2021. 

(7) Many statements and conclusions are unclear to me. E.g., “Surprisingly, for these five distinct CIL algorithms, the accuracy remains relatively unchanged across all incremental stages, despite a few minor variations.” Could this be due to the balance/trade-off of forgetting and learning more features with each new task? See above. I suspect a lot of your observations may be due to pre-training. DER is slightly different because it protects the features learned in the past. [1,2,3] also protect old features. 

(8) Regarding the two proposed variations of DER, they do not really make a major difference in results. They are minor variations, e.g., some previous methods have already tried to fix the earlier layers. Please give the error bar.

(9) You should experimentally compare with the existing methods (including the above suggested references) using some common benchmarks, e.g., CIFAR datasets and tinyImageNet, so that it is easier to see the difference in results compared to others.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is readable with some work. 
Novelty is not much. The analysis and experiments have some issues. 
Reproducibility should be fine.
content.summary_of_the_review: I have several problems with the experimental analysis. The inspired modifications to DER are not compared with many more appreciate baselines. Overall, in my opinion, the novelty of the paper is not much.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
